subject: ela
intro: This quiz checks whether you can compare and contrast reading a story, drama, or poem with hearing or watching a version of the same text. Each question gives you the written words and describes the audio, video, or live version in words. Choose the single best answer.

items.prompt:
Read the line: "Mara said she was fine, and she smiled as she said it." In a film version, the actor playing Mara lets her voice shake and her eyes fill with tears as she says the line. What can the film show that the written line by itself does not?

A) That Mara is not really fine, because her shaking voice and tears reveal hidden sadness
B) That Mara said the word "fine" and then smiled
C) That the film is the same as the text because both use Mara's words
D) The exact thoughts running through Mara's mind in that moment
items.answer: A) That Mara is not really fine, because her shaking voice and tears reveal hidden sadness

steps: The written line only reports Mara's words and her smile, so a reader has to guess how she truly feels.
The film adds a shaking voice and tears, which let the audience see her hidden sadness. That is what the film shows that the words alone do not, so A is correct.
B is wrong because it only repeats what the written line already states and names nothing the film adds.
C is wrong because it treats the two versions as identical and misses the difference the actor's performance creates.
D is wrong because the film shows feelings through voice and face but cannot directly reveal the exact words in Mara's mind; that is something print does, not film.

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: "The old house stood silent at the end of the lane, its windows dark." In an audio recording of this story, soft eerie music plays under the narrator's voice during this sentence. What has the audio version added that the written text does not include?

A) Eerie background music, which makes the house feel frightening
B) The detail that the windows are dark
C) Nothing, because the audio uses the same words as the text
D) A description of who used to live in the house
items.answer: A) Eerie background music, which makes the house feel frightening

steps: The written text gives only silence, the lane, and dark windows. It contains no sound.
The audio adds eerie music, a tool print cannot provide, and that music makes the house feel scary before anything frightening happens. So A is correct.
B is wrong because dark windows are already in the written text and were not added by the audio.
C is wrong because it claims the version is the same as the text and ignores the new music that changes the experience.
D is wrong because neither the text nor the described audio mentions who lived in the house.

items.prompt:
Read the description: "The dragon was larger than any creature the villagers had ever seen." In a movie version, the dragon is shown as a green, smoke-breathing beast the size of a barn. What is one true difference between reading this line and watching the movie?

A) When reading, each person imagines the dragon's exact size and color, but the movie fixes one image for everyone
B) The reading lets you hear the dragon roar, but the movie does not
C) There is no difference, because both versions describe the same dragon
D) The written line already tells you the dragon is green and the size of a barn
items.answer: A) When reading, each person imagines the dragon's exact size and color, but the movie fixes one image for everyone

steps: The written line says only that the dragon is very large, so each reader pictures its color and exact size differently.
The movie shows one fixed image, a green beast the size of a barn, the same for everyone watching. That contrast in imagination is the real difference, so A is correct.
B is wrong because a written text cannot make you hear a roar; sound belongs to the movie, not the page.
C is wrong because it claims there is no difference and ignores how each medium handles the image.
D is wrong because the written line never gives the dragon's color or compares it to a barn; only the movie supplies those details.

items.prompt:
Read the stage direction and line from a drama: "TOM (quietly): I never wanted any of this." In a live performance, the actor playing Tom turns away from the other characters and lowers his head just before he speaks. How does the live version's choice change this moment compared with reading the script?

A) The turning away and lowered head let the audience see Tom's shame and his wish to hide, which the words alone do not show
B) The live version is better simply because watching a play is more fun than reading
C) The live version removes Tom's line so the audience never hears him speak
D) The script already tells the reader that Tom turns away in shame before he speaks
items.answer: A) The turning away and lowered head let the audience see Tom's shame and his wish to hide, which the words alone do not show

steps: On the page the reader learns only that Tom speaks quietly. The script gives no body movement.
In the live version the actor turns away and lowers his head, and these actions let the audience read his shame and his urge to hide. That added meaning is the change, so A is correct.
B is wrong because it judges the version by personal fun, not by what the performance actually conveys.
C is wrong because the actor still speaks the line; nothing in the description says the line was cut.
D is wrong because it blurs the version with the text: the turning away comes from the actor, not from the printed script.

items.prompt:
Read the poem lines: "Down, down, down the rain came, / drumming on the tin roof all night." In an audio version, a reader speaks these lines slowly while a steady tapping sound plays behind the words. How does hearing this version compare with reading it silently?

A) The audio adds a real tapping sound and a slow pace, so the listener hears the rain's rhythm instead of only picturing it
B) The audio and the silent reading give exactly the same experience because the words match
C) The silent reading lets the reader hear the actual tapping, while the audio only describes it
D) The audio is worse because reading a poem is always more boring than hearing one
items.answer: A) The audio adds a real tapping sound and a slow pace, so the listener hears the rain's rhythm instead of only picturing it

steps: Reading silently, you notice the repeated word "down" and imagine the rain on the roof.
The audio adds an actual tapping sound and a slow speaking pace, so you hear the rhythm rather than only picturing it. That makes the steady, sleepy feeling stronger, so A is correct.
B is wrong because it claims the experiences are identical and ignores the sound and pace the audio adds.
C is wrong because silent reading cannot make you hear tapping; sound belongs to the audio, not the page.
D is wrong because it rests on personal preference, not on what each version conveys.

items.prompt:
Read the excerpt: "In her mind, Lena replayed every word of the argument, sure she had ruined everything." A film of this scene shows Lena sitting alone on her bed and staring at the floor, but adds no narration. For showing what Lena is actually thinking, which version is more effective, and why?

A) The written text, because it states Lena's exact thoughts and her fear that she ruined everything
B) The film, because it shows everything and is always more complete than a book
C) The film, because seeing Lena on her bed proves what each word in her mind is
D) Neither, because the text and the film give the audience the very same information
items.answer: A) The written text, because it states Lena's exact thoughts and her fear that she ruined everything

steps: The written text directly reports Lena's inner words: she replays the argument and fears she ruined everything.

The film shows her sitting and staring, which signals she is upset, but with no narration it cannot reveal the exact thoughts in her mind. So for inner thinking the text is more effective, making A correct.
B is wrong because it assumes the film is always more complete and ignores that print is what reveals unspoken thoughts.
C is wrong because an image of Lena on her bed cannot prove the specific words she is thinking.
D is wrong because the two versions do not give the same information: only the text states her exact thoughts.

items.prompt:
Read the passage: "Jonah stood at the edge of the diving board, the pool far below. His friends called for him to jump. He told them he was not scared at all. He took one slow step forward, then stopped. The wind pushed at his back. He told himself the water was warm and the height was nothing." In a film version, the camera looks straight down from behind Jonah to show how high the board is, the crowd noise fades to near silence, and the actor's hands grip the rail and tremble while he calls out, "I'm not scared!" Which statement best compares the two versions of this moment?

A) Both versions show Jonah's brave words, but the film's downward camera, silence, and trembling hands reveal a fear that the passage only hints at
B) The film and the passage are identical because Jonah says he is not scared in each one
C) The film proves Jonah is truly unafraid, since he shouts "I'm not scared!" out loud
D) The passage lets the reader hear the crowd fall silent, while the film cannot show silence
items.answer: A) Both versions show Jonah's brave words, but the film's downward camera, silence, and trembling hands reveal a fear that the passage only hints at

steps: A good comparison names a similarity and a difference grounded in both versions.

Both versions keep Jonah's brave claim that he is not scared, which is the similarity. The film then adds a steep downward camera, fading crowd noise, and trembling hands, and together these choices expose the fear that the passage only suggests through his slow step and stopping. That makes A correct.
B is wrong because it treats the versions as identical and ignores how the film's images and sound add fear.
C is wrong because shouting "I'm not scared" does not prove he is unafraid; his trembling hands point the opposite way.
D is wrong because it credits print with hearing silence, a sound effect that belongs to the film, not the page.

items.prompt:
Read the passage: "The letter arrived on a gray morning. Priya read it twice, then folded it slowly and set it on the table. For a long moment she said nothing. Outside, a bird kept singing, bright and cheerful, as if nothing in the world had changed. She picked up her coat and walked to the door." In an audio version, the narrator reads in a flat, heavy voice, a single low piano note sounds when the letter is folded, and the cheerful birdsong is played loud and clear under the lines about the bird. How does the audio version's interpretation shape this moment compared with reading it silently?

A) The flat voice and low piano stress Priya's sorrow, while the loud cheerful birdsong sharpens the contrast between her grief and the untouched world
B) The audio changes nothing important, since it reads the same words the passage already contains
C) The audio is automatically the better version because hearing a story is always richer than reading one
D) The passage itself plays the piano note and the birdsong for the reader, so the audio adds no new sound
items.answer: A) The flat voice and low piano stress Priya's sorrow, while the loud cheerful birdsong sharpens the contrast between her grief and the untouched world

steps: Reading silently, you notice the gray morning, Priya's silence, and the cheerful bird, and you supply the tone yourself.

The audio interprets the moment: a flat, heavy voice and a low piano note press Priya's sorrow forward, and the loud cheerful birdsong heightens the gap between her grief and a world that goes on as before. Connecting those choices to that effect makes A correct.
B is wrong because it claims the audio changes nothing, ignoring how voice, music, and the loud birdsong shape feeling.
C is wrong because it rests on a blanket preference rather than on what these specific choices convey.
D is wrong because it credits the printed passage with playing the piano and birdsong, when those sounds are added only by the audio version.
